description: We are MEGED, a team of five from Lomé, Togo, building an interactive 3D browser game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Our goal: win, and make space engineering real and fun for students. We bring game development, data analysis, physics simulation, UI/UX, security, pitch and gameplay testing. We are looking for ONE more teammate: a graphic designer, motion designer or video maker for our visual identity and demo video. We work in French and English.
summary:
SANKOFA-1 is a 3D web game in which one player, or a team of up to four players sharing one screen, designs, launches and operates a lunar science mission. Players choose an objective with numbered requirements, then build the spacecraft: instruments, power, antenna, memory, engine, propellant, orbit and launch vehicle. Every choice shows its cost before the click, in kilograms, watts, credits, data and days. The mission is then flown: launch, translunar injection, trajectory correction, unexpected events, orbit insertion and science operations. A final report shows which requirements were met and how each decision changed the score.
The challenge asks for a game where engineering trade-offs stop being abstract. In SANKOFA-1, one more instrument means more mass, more propellant (rocket equation), more power, more data and fewer credits. A failed mission is never a dead end: players keep their design, change it and fly again, the meaning of the Akan word "sankofa".
It matters because students rarely get to make these decisions themselves. The game runs in a browser with no account, for a classroom with one screen where four students take four engineering roles and negotiate.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SANKOFA-1 covers a complete lunar mission in six phases. Each phase follows four steps: inform, decide (with the cost shown before the choice), simulate, explain.

1. Design: players pick a mission objective with three numbered requirements, following the requirements-first approach of the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook. They compose the spacecraft from a catalogue of science instruments and subsystems, choose a lunar orbit and a launch vehicle. A compatibility light turns red when the total mass exceeds what the launcher can carry.

2. Launch: launch in the window or delay, at a cost.

3. Flight: translunar injection, then a trajectory correction where correcting late costs more.

4. Orbit insertion: the burn happens behind the Moon, during a radio blackout.

5. Operations: players share power and antenna time between taking measurements and sending data home. Only data received on Earth counts.

6. Mission report: requirements met or missed with the reason, a score in four parts, and an impact table listing each key decision with its effect in points. Players can go back to Design and fly again.

Unexpected events, such as an underperforming engine or a solar flare, force real trade-offs with the cost shown before the choice.

HOW IT WORKS

The game uses real equations in a simplified model: the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation for delta-v and the effect of every added kilogram, a Hohmann transfer from low Earth orbit to the Moon, and power and data budgets per orbit. The 3D scene is built with Three.js; some sizes and distances are exaggerated so the Earth, the Moon and the spacecraft stay readable.

Team mode: up to four players share one screen, each with a role (Mission and Budget, Science, Spacecraft, Communications and Data) with its own priority. In solo mode, one player holds all four roles.

Score: objectives met (40%), science value of data received on Earth (30%), resource management (20%), collaboration (10%).

Two fictional characters guide the players: Aminata, the chief engineer, and AKILI, the flight director, who explains each choice and each failure with the numbers of the current game. Their lines are written in advance by the team; no AI model runs during play.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Everything is connected: mass, power, budget, data, communications and time pull against each other in one design. Several designs can succeed, and the report shows why. Failure teaches, with an explanation in numbers. Built for classrooms: one screen, up to four roles, no installation, no account. We want a student to understand in one session that adding mass costs propellant, that the orbit changes everything, and that a mission is decided as a team, and young people in Africa and everywhere to see themselves running a space mission.

TOOLS

TypeScript, Three.js, Vite, Python (reference physics model), Meshy (3D instrument models), Kenney Space Kit (CC0), Figtree font (SIL OFL), Git and GitHub, Netlify. AI tools: Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini, Meshy (see references).
